title: Pray differently
hook: pray not "let me get this" but "let me not crave it," not "let me be rid of it" but "let me not fear" (Meditations 9.40)

segments.voice: Yesterday: rushing river. Your line was the smallest thing. What small thing moved forward? Day six hundred twelve.

Late at night, the asking comes. Let the test come back clear. Let me get the job. Let this pain go away. Let my kid be okay. People of every faith, and people of none, find themselves sending wishes like these out into the dark. Marcus did too. Near the end of book nine he wrote a short reflection on his own prayers, and it turns the asking around. Today: pray differently.
screen: `LATE AT NIGHT, THE ASKING.` → `LET THIS PASS.` → `PRAY DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: First, the argument. Either the gods have power or they don't, Marcus writes. If they don't, why pray at all? If they do, why not pray for the power not to fear these things, not to crave them, not to grieve over them, rather than praying only that they come or don't come? Second, the objection. Someone might say: but the gods put that in my own power. Then, Marcus answers, isn't it better to use what's in your power with freedom than to strain like a slave after what isn't? And who told you the gods don't help us even with what's in our power? Third, his examples. One person prays: how can I win that woman? You, he tells himself: how can I stop wanting to? Another: how can I be rid of this? You: how can I stop needing to be rid of it? Another: how can I not lose my little son? You: how can I not be afraid to lose him? Turn your prayers this way, he says, and see what comes. Fourth, reading him fairly. Marcus is writing to himself, a Stoic, about his own prayers. He isn't speaking for anyone else's. People in many traditions pray for healing and for their children, and many also pray for courage and peace in the same breath. And the little son is not abstract. Marcus and his wife Faustina lost a number of their children young.
screen: `EITHER THE GODS CAN, OR THEY CAN'T.` · `USE WHAT'S IN YOUR POWER, FREELY.` · `NOT LOSE HIM, OR NOT FEAR LOSING HIM.` · `HIS OWN PRAYERS, NO ONE ELSE'S.` · then, large: `LET ME NOT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Name one wish you've been carrying, something you want to happen or stop happening. Hold it honestly; you don't have to give it up. Now try Marcus's turn on it. Underneath the wish, notice the fear or the craving that comes with it. If you pray, you might bring both to your prayer, the wish and the calm, in whatever words your own tradition gives you. If you don't, simply hold the turn: less fear of this. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Pray differently. Marcus's turn: not only let me get this, but let me not crave it; not only save me from this, but let me not fear it. Today's word.
Your line: let me not fear. When a wish or a worry tightens today, notice the fear underneath it, and say your line. Day six hundred twelve.

screen: `DAY 612 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WILL YOU EVER BE GOOD?`

howItsDone: Readers who take up this entry often notice the fear or craving beneath a hope, and those who pray sometimes ask for steadiness alongside the outcome they want, in the words of their own tradition.

pairs: pray not to fear, crave, or grieve
not lose him, or not fear losing him

myth: Marcus tells everyone to stop praying for outcomes
he's writing to himself about his own prayers, and speaks for no one else's.
in his third example, one person prays not to lose a son, and Marcus prays not to fear losing him
that's the last of his three examples.

fork.setup: you're Marcus. your little son is sick. how does his notebook say to turn the prayer?
options: how can I not lose him?
how can I not be afraid to lose him?
fork.reveal: he contrasts asking not to lose his little son with asking not to be afraid of losing him. Marcus and Faustina lost a number of their children young.

original.note: Greek: I pray, I ask, I wish. Marcus's turn changes what the asking is for.

trapdoor: what you thought: a philosopher dismissing prayer.
what it means: Marcus keeps praying, but asks for freedom from fear and craving, not only for the outcome.
what a scholar hears: the entry is a short dilemma argument, either the gods can act or they can't, a form Marcus uses again and again in the Meditations.
recall: no stepping in the same river twice
the ruling part, the steering center

notes: 9.40 paraphrased, including the three examples (the woman, being rid of something, the little son) and 'Turn thy prayers this way, and see what comes' (Long). Confirm.
No new prayer is written; the practice invites listeners who pray to use their own tradition's words.
Marcus and Faustina had many children, several of whom died young; confirm the wording 'a number of their children' against standard biographies.
Hook's index field contains straight double quotes from the outline; kept exactly as the index has it.
